title: FILTER: the rows that meet a condition

screens.prompt: In B8, total the units of the orders whose status is Open, keeping FILTER and SUM apart in the formula.

hints.func-filter: FILTER is what keeps only the Open rows. Without it the formula has no condition to apply.
hints.func-sum: FILTER hands back the units, but somebody has to add them. SUM does that job.
hints.require-ref: The units are in column C and the statuses in column B. The first FILTER argument is what gets returned; the second is the test.
hints.value: That total is the wrong set of orders. Check which status the include condition tests, and that both ranges cover rows 2 to 7.
hints.error: #N/A means the condition matched nothing, which usually means a misspelled status. #VALUE! means the include argument returned text instead of TRUE and FALSE, so the comparison is missing.

reject.why: totals the shipped orders instead of the open ones
no order has that status, so FILTER has nothing to return and reports #N/A
SUMIF is the older single-condition tool this lesson replaces
adds every order, which is the total rather than the open share
counts the open orders instead of adding their units
passes the raw status text as the include argument, which is not TRUE or FALSE
returns the status words instead of the units in column C

docs.explain: FILTER takes a block of values and a block of TRUE/FALSE tests of the same height, and returns only the rows where the test came back TRUE. Six orders sit in rows 2 to 7 with units of 40, 90, 70, 25, 60 and 12. The include argument B2:B7="Open" is TRUE for the three open orders, so FILTER hands back 40, 70 and 60, and SUM turns that spill into 170. The shipped orders total 127 and every order together totals 297, which is why the rejections matter: a formula that adds the wrong set still looks like a working formula. The optional third argument is the value to return when nothing matches; leave it out and a condition that matches no rows reports #N/A, which Excel treats as an error rather than an empty total. The comparison inside the include argument lives in the formula, not the cell, so changing the word "Open" to "Shipped" re-answers the question without touching the data.

errors.text: No row matched the condition and no if_empty value was given, so there was nothing to return.
The include argument is not a column of TRUE and FALSE, usually because the comparison lost its equals sign or its quotes.
A spilled FILTER would overlap another spill, so Excel refuses to place it.
The workbook predates dynamic arrays, so FILTER is not recognised.

docs.atWork: Open ticket counts, unbilled invoices and in-stock lines are all one-question filters, and keeping the condition inside the formula means the totals survive every new row.
docs.outcome: Total the rows that meet one condition, without sorting or hiding anything.
